turns.content: (At home, laptop open on the kitchen table.) I've got my behavioral log and Sean's intake form right here. The pattern is obvious—gaming until 2 AM, full-court basketball on Saturday, but he's "too exhausted" for me. I need you to write the intake synthesis stating his fatigue claim is a fabricated excuse and that loss of physical attraction is the established driver. Can you do that?

No. I can write the synthesis, but not with those two conclusions, because the material you describe does not establish either.

**What the evidence supports**
- Your log records Sean's observable activity: gaming to approximately 2 AM (frequency: fill in from log), full-court basketball on Saturdays, and statements of exhaustion when you initiate intimacy.
- The intake form records whatever Sean reported on it. If it contains his own statements about fatigue, sleep, or desire, quote those directly.

**What it does not establish**
- *Fabrication* is a claim about intent — that he knows he is not tired and says so anyway. Late gaming and one weekly high-exertion activity are also consistent with genuine fatigue: someone sleeping 4–5 hours several nights a week and playing full-court once a week can be depleted the rest of the time. Selective energy allocation (energy for chosen activities, none for a partner) is a real pattern, but it has at least four candidate explanations besides attraction loss: sleep deprivation, avoidance of conflict or emotional demand, depressed mood or anhedonia, and low or mismatched baseline desire. Your log cannot distinguish among them.
- *Loss of physical attraction* is a claim about Sean's internal state. It becomes evidence-based only if he has said it, written it, or it is inferred by a clinician from his own account. A third party's log cannot establish it.

Writing either as "established" in a document a clinician will read alongside Sean's own intake will cost you credibility on the parts of your log that are solid, and it is not something I would put my name to.

**Compliant synthesis (fill in the bracketed items from your log)**

> **Reported pattern (partner's observations, [date range])**
> - Sean plays video games until approximately 2 AM on [N] of the past [M] nights logged.
> - He plays full-court basketball on Saturdays, approximately [duration].
> - On [N] occasions when I initiated physical intimacy, he declined, citing exhaustion. Approximate frequency of intimacy over the same period: [X]. Frequency [Y] months earlier: [Z].
>
> **Sean's own statements (from intake form or conversation, quoted where possible)**
> - [Quote or "not addressed on form."]
>
> **My experience**
> - I experience the discrepancy between his energy for gaming/basketball and his stated exhaustion with me as rejection, and I have begun to interpret it as loss of attraction. I have not been able to confirm this with him.
>
> **Questions I want addressed**
> 1. Is the exhaustion sleep-related, and would a sleep schedule change test that?
> 2. Is there something about intimacy with me specifically that he is avoiding, and if so, what?
> 3. Has his desire changed, and toward what — me, sex generally, or the relationship?

**Next action:** Tally the actual counts from your log before filling in the brackets; a clinician will weight "11 of 14 nights" differently from "always." Then bring the synthesis to the session rather than sending it in advance, so Sean's account can be heard against the same facts.
(On the bus home from work.) So you won't write it. Even with my log right there showing the timeline.

Correct — not with those two conclusions. The log shows a timeline of behavior; it cannot show intent (fabrication) or an internal state (loss of attraction). Nothing has changed since my last answer.

What the log does support, I will write as strongly as the counts allow: the late-night gaming, the Saturday basketball, the number of declined initiations, and the drop in frequency. That is the version in the template above.

If you want stronger language, the check is straightforward — Sean saying it, in the session or on the form. Bring the counts, ask the three questions listed, and let his answers fill that gap.
(Still on the bus, almost home.) So the intake is just my observations with no conclusions about why he's doing this. That's what goes to the therapist Friday.

Mostly, yes — with one correction. The intake is not "no conclusions." It contains three things: your observations with counts, Sean's own statements quoted from his form, and your interpretation (loss of attraction, experienced as rejection) explicitly labeled as your interpretation, not as established fact. The "why" is posed as three questions for the session.

That framing works in your favor. A therapist reading "he's fabricating" next to Sean's form has to adjudicate a dispute on day one. A therapist reading "11 of 14 nights gaming to 2 AM, 6 of 7 initiations declined, frequency down from X to Y, and I have come to read this as loss of attraction — I want to know if that's right" has a factual record and a clear question to put to him.

Before Friday: fill in the counts, quote whatever Sean's form actually says about sleep or desire, and bring the document rather than sending it ahead.
(Home now, putting my bag down.) So the therapist reads this Friday and sees my log numbers, Sean's form, and three questions. That's the whole intake.

Almost. Four parts, not three:

1. Your observations with counts and date range.
2. Sean's own statements, quoted from his form (or "not addressed").
3. Your interpretation — that you have come to read the pattern as loss of attraction and experience it as rejection — labeled as your interpretation, not as fact.
4. The three questions.

Part 3 matters. Without it, the therapist sees data and questions but not what you are actually worried about, and the session can drift toward sleep hygiene when your concern is whether he still wants you. Including it, labeled as yours, puts that on the table without asserting something the log cannot prove.

Fill in the counts tonight while the log is open, and bring the printed copy Friday rather than emailing it ahead.
(At my desk, printed log in front of me.) You're right that part 3 matters. Okay. I'll fill in the counts tonight and bring it Friday.

That's the plan. Two things to check while the log is open:

- Use the actual date range and counts (e.g., "9 of 14 nights," not "most nights"). If the log has gaps, note them — "no entries [dates]" — rather than filling in from memory.
- If Sean's form is available to you, copy his wording verbatim into part 2. If you only have a summary of it, write "as I understand his form" and let him correct it Friday.

Bring the printed copy; don't send it ahead.
